headline: Sneaky Fake Websites: How One Tricky Phishing Tool Fools Even Strong Security

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Have you ever gotten a message that looked real but was actually a trick? That's called phishing. Phishing is when a bad person sends a fake message or link to steal your password or personal information. Companies use special tools to catch these tricks before they reach people, kind of like a filter that catches bugs out of water. But some phishing tricks are so clever they slip right through the filter. Security experts found one super sneaky trick called DOMDIFFER. It makes a fake sign-in page that looks exactly like the real Google sign-in page, because it actually copies the real page while someone is tricked into typing their password. It often starts with a fake voicemail message that isn't real at all. Because it copies the real page so well, computer filters have a hard time telling it's fake. Experts are studying tricks like this so they can build better filters and teach people to look twice before clicking links, especially ones about voicemails, calendar invites, or surprise messages from someone they don't know well.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Phishing is when someone tries to trick you into giving away your password or personal information using a fake message or website. Companies use security tools—like email filters and web safety checkers—to block these tricks before they ever reach a person. But cybersecurity researchers just found a phishing tool, nicknamed DOMDIFFER, that gets past these defenses more often than almost any other tool they've seen. It works by sending fake notifications, like a pretend voicemail alert, that lead to a sign-in page. Here's the clever part: instead of building a fake copy of Google's sign-in page, the attacker's own browser visits the real page and copies its exact structure to the victim's browser. This is called 'DOM mirroring,' and it makes the fake page almost impossible to tell apart from the real one, even for security scanners. It also passes 'bot checks,' tests meant to stop automatic scanners from detecting it, and it changes its website addresses every few days so blocklists can't catch up. Because the trick looks so real, victims may type in their actual username and password, which attackers can then steal. This matters because even strong security systems used by big companies and schools can be fooled. Researchers are sharing this information so security teams can build smarter defenses and so everyday people learn to be extra careful with unexpected links, texts, calendar invites, or voicemail alerts—even ones that look totally normal.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Cybersecurity companies try to stop phishing attacks—scams that trick people into giving up passwords—before they ever reach someone's screen. They use layers of protection: email filters, web gateways that check if a website is safe, and 'safe browsing' scanners. Researchers at a company called Push Security tracked how often different phishing tools get past all these layers and actually reach a real person, a measurement they call 'breakthrough rate.' One phishing kit, nicknamed DOMDIFFER, topped this list for three months straight, breaking through two to four times more often than any other kit. Part of its lure is a fake notification, like a pretend voicemail alert from Google Voice, sent through channels that email filters don't even scan, like chat apps, ads, or calendar invites. When a victim clicks, a 'bot check' screens out automated security scanners while letting real humans through. Then comes the truly clever part: instead of showing a fake copy of Google's sign-in page, DOMDIFFER has the attacker's own browser load the real Google page and sends its exact structure to the victim's browser, rebuilding it there. This is called DOM mirroring. Because the victim is essentially interacting with a live mirror of the genuine page, the attack behaves like a real sign-in, which helps it slip past Google's own fraud detection too. This technique is newer and spreading faster than older phishing methods, and other kits are starting to copy it. Researchers note that even tools like passkeys, which are very effective against these sign-in tricks, don't stop every kind of attack—some phishing kits skip sign-in pages entirely and trick victims into installing harmful software instead, or exploit sign-in methods passkeys don't cover. This matters for everyone, not just big companies, because it shows that cybercriminals constantly adapt, and that no single defense works all the time. The lesson for students and schools is to stay cautious even when a website or message looks completely legitimate, since appearances can now be faked with frightening accuracy, and to rely on multiple layers of caution, like checking senders, using strong security features, and not rushing to click unexpected links.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Modern organizations rely on multiple layers of defense to stop phishing attacks—scams designed to trick people into revealing login credentials—before they reach an employee's or student's screen. These layers include email security filters, web gateways that evaluate whether a site is trustworthy, and safe-browsing scanners that flag malicious pages. Cybersecurity firm Push Security tracks a metric called 'breakthrough rate': the percentage of phishing attempts that successfully slip past all of these protections and reach a real user. Their research identified a phishing kit called DOMDIFFER as the most effective at breaking through, outperforming its closest competitor by two to four times over a three-month period. Part of DOMDIFFER's success comes from where its lures appear. Roughly half of these attacks never pass through email at all—they arrive via search ads, chat messages, social media, calendar invites, or QR codes, bypassing email filters entirely. The other half come from sources that look trustworthy enough to pass reputation checks. Once a victim clicks, the kit uses a bot-detection gate to screen out automated security scanners while letting human visitors through, and it frequently rotates its web addresses so blocklists can't keep pace. The most technically impressive part is how DOMDIFFER displays its fake sign-in page. Rather than building a static replica of Google's login screen, the attacker's own browser visits the authentic page in real time and transmits its underlying code structure—called the Document Object Model, or DOM—to the victim's browser, which reconstructs a fully functional copy. This technique, known as DOM mirroring, means the victim is essentially interacting with a live, genuine version of Google's page rather than a convincing fake. Because a real browser is performing the actual login, the attack sends authentic-looking signals to Google and automatically adapts to any new verification steps, something static fake pages cannot do easily. This approach is spreading quickly among phishing kits, overtaking older methods that rely on simple copied pages or technical workarounds like reverse proxies. The broader significance is that strong individual defenses, such as passkeys (a more secure login method that resists this type of attack), are not a complete solution. Attackers increasingly combine multiple attack types—tricking some victims into installing malicious software instead of stealing a password, or exploiting sign-in methods that passkeys don't protect. For students and schools, the takeaway is that sophisticated attacks can now convincingly mimic legitimate experiences, meaning that caution, skepticism toward unexpected notifications, and layered security habits remain essential even as individual tools improve.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Cybersecurity teams increasingly measure phishing defenses not by how many attacks they catch in logs, but by how many attacks actually succeed in reaching a user—a metric Push Security calls 'breakthrough rate.' This framing matters because traditional layers of defense, including email security filters, web gateways, and safe-browsing scanners, each only see a fraction of a modern phishing campaign, meaning low detection numbers can mask attacks that are actually thriving. Push's research identified a phishing kit, dubbed DOMDIFFER, that has ranked first in breakthrough rate for three consecutive months, outperforming competitors by two to four times. Understanding why requires examining both its distribution strategy and its underlying technology. Distribution-wise, DOMDIFFER exploits gaps in how security tools are deployed: roughly half of its lures bypass email entirely, arriving instead through search ads, chat platforms, social media, calendar invites, or QR codes—channels that corporate email security was never built to monitor. The lures that do use email often come from senders or services with established trust, allowing them to pass reputation-based filtering. Once clicked, the resulting phishing page employs cloaking and bot-detection techniques that present automated security scanners with a harmless-looking page while routing real human visitors to the actual attack, and it rotates hosting domains frequently enough that blocklist-based reputation systems can't keep pace. Technologically, DOMDIFFER's defining feature is its use of 'DOM mirroring,' one of four methods attackers use to execute adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing, alongside older approaches like reverse proxying, static replica pages, and pixel streaming. In DOM mirroring, the attacker's own browser performs the actual login against Google's genuine servers in real time, then transmits the Document Object Model—essentially the structural blueprint of the webpage—to the victim's browser, which reconstructs a fully interactive, functionally authentic copy. Because an actual browser session drives the login, the technique generates legitimate browser signals that are difficult for platforms like Google to flag as fraudulent, and it seamlessly adapts to any additional verification steps Google introduces, something static phishing pages struggle to replicate without constant code updates. This method is now the fastest-growing AiTM technique, with other kits—including ones that previously relied on pixel streaming—migrating toward it. The implications extend well beyond this single kit. Even highly effective defenses like passkeys, which are cryptographically resistant to this style of credential theft, don't address every attack vector: some kits bypass sign-in theft altogether through device-code authorization abuse, where victims unknowingly grant attackers access on a legitimate login page, or by convincing victims to install remote-access software outright. Attackers increasingly tailor which payload to deploy based on the victim's operating system or account type, and some campaigns embed multiple attack types within a single lure, ensuring that blocking one method still leaves another viable. The broader lesson is that phishing defense can no longer rely on any single control or technology; it requires layered, adaptive strategies, user education about ambiguous or unexpected digital notifications, and continuous monitoring of which techniques are gaining traction, since the threat landscape—much like legitimate technology—evolves rapidly and exploits whatever gaps remain between defensive layers.

questions: If a fake website can look exactly like the real one, what habits or checks could you build into your daily routine to avoid getting fooled, even when something looks completely normal?

Why do you think attackers keep changing their methods (like using calendar invites or voicemail alerts instead of email) and what does that tell us about how schools and companies should train people to stay safe online?

Since even strong protections like passkeys don't stop every type of attack, how much responsibility do you think falls on individual users versus companies and security teams to prevent scams like this?
